newsitem.title: UK: Rugby union's Five Nations back in business.
newsitem.headline: Rugby union's Five Nations back in business.

text.p: The Five Nations championship, threatened with extinction in rugby union's haste to bankroll the new professional era, has been saved "for the foreseeable future", it was announced on Thursday.

The tournament, which dates back to 1909, will take place as scheduled starting in January following a last-ditch agreement between the home unions four days before England's expulsion was due to be rubber-stamped at a meeting in Dublin.

Details of the breakthrough in a bitter dispute which arose when England sold their own television rights to Five Nations matches, ignoring an agreement with their opponents to negotiate collectively, will not made public until Monday.

But there will be widespread relief the "jewel in the crown' of northern hemisphere rugby is not to disappear, a scenario which looked probable when England were thrown out by their European partners last July.

A statement issued on behalf of the English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish unions, who also kept their French counterparts fully informed, revealed that an eight-hour meeting in Bristol late on Wednesday had resulted in "an accord which has saved the Five Nations championship for the coming season and for the foreseeable future."

Rugby Football Union (RFU) secretary Tony Hallett hopes the resolution of the long-running dispute will ease the way to a settlement of the parallel row between his union and the senior English clubs.

The national squad boycotted a training session on Thursday and the clubs are still threatening to split from the RFU next month unless their demands for greater power and a bigger share of the "new money' coming into the game are met.
"Resolving the Five Nations issue must help in the jigsaw of problems that we face," Hallett admitted.
"It is a major achievement by the negotiators. The competition is special and attractive. It is a weight off our shoulders and a help that we are not fighting battles on so many fronts."
Lawrence Dallaglio, England flanker and a contender to be the side's new captain, commented: "It is very welcome news. Everyone wants England in the Five Nations.
"It is difficult to comment in the long term, but England players need to start training and preparing for the test against Italy in November."
There is still a question mark over how much, if any, ground RFU negotiators have conceded regarding how big a share of television revenue each country will receive.

They insist the 87.5 million pounds ($137.3 million) contract they have signed with satellite television operator BSkyB is legally binding and have always claimed they deserve by far the largest share because they have more players and clubs to administer.

News of the latest development was sudden and unexpected. RFU treasurer Colin Herridge interrupted the official launch of the Rothmans' Rugby Union Yearbook by entering the room, waving a piece of paper in the air and announcing: "We have peace in our time".

The RFU still face a struggle to persuade their league one and two clubs to rejoin the Twickenham fold, with Hallett hinting their may be offered an extra one million pounds in addition to the 4.2 million they have already been promised.

Yet for players and supporters to whom the Five Nations is not so much a sports event as an annual social rite, there is finally light at the end of a tunnel previously as black as Jonah Lomu's jersey.
As Hallett concluded: "I hope politics can take a back seat and we can get on with playing the game."
